title: Two Ways of Thinking, Two Explanation Challenges
author: Science of Explanation
summary: Drawing on Daniel Kahneman's dual-process theory, this article applies the System 1 / System 2 framework to the challenge of explanation — specifically, what it means to explain something to someone who is engaged in automatic, fast thinking versus someone who has activated deliberate, slow thinking. System 1 thinking is rapid, effortless, and pattern-driven; it processes information below conscious awareness but makes predictable errors and is easily overloaded by unfamiliarity. System 2 thinking is deliberate, effortful, and constructive; it can handle novel information and build new understanding, but has strict capacity limits. The article frames these as two distinct explanation challenges: earning enough attention to get information into conscious processing (the System 1 challenge), and managing cognitive load effectively enough to allow System 2 to build lasting understanding (the System 2 challenge). Using the recurring story of a patient named Olivia who remembers only 'eat more fiber' from a doctor's visit, the author illustrates why so much well-intentioned explanation fails to produce learning. The piece is part of a series on the science of explanation, relevant to teachers, communicators, and anyone who needs to transfer understanding reliably.
points: The two explanation challenges are distinct and sequential: you must first earn System 1's attention (get past automatic filtering) before System 2 can engage with deliberate understanding.

System 1's key characteristic for explainers is selectivity: it filters information through existing patterns and expectations, so explanations that violate expectation or lack a clear hook will be discarded before conscious processing begins.

System 2's key constraint is capacity: it can only hold a limited amount of new information at once, so explaining too much — even to an attentive audience — guarantees that most of it will not be retained.

The 'eat more fiber' example is pedagogically powerful: Olivia remembered the one thing that had existing context (she'd heard about fiber before), not the most medically important recommendation — prior knowledge determines what sticks.

The practical implication for teachers is that successful explanation is not primarily about clarity of delivery but about managing attention and cognitive load simultaneously — two distinct problems that require different solutions.
quotes: The most recent posts about attention, context, and gist are now under the umbrella of Kahneman’s System 1 or “fast” thinking. In the post below, I’m using the recurring story of Olivia to set the stage for the next phase and a deeper dive into System 2 or “slow” thinking.
Her existing knowledge (context [ ]) helped her evaluate what was said. This created a substrate for memory to form, but this is only the beginning.
This is where we make a conscious effort to think something through. We apply reason and knowledge to construct an understanding of what we have experienced.

This deliberate reflection is System 2 thinking, and it can create action and long-term memories. This wasn’t necessarily a conscious decision, but a matter of competing priorities and a limited ability to process everything.

In fact, many researchers consider System 2 to be distinctly human. Having captured Olivia's attention and been deemed meaningful, the fiber advice became available for more deliberate thought, the kind of conscious reflection that System 2 makes possible.

It became part of cognitive science in the 1970s and gained widespread awareness from Kahneman’s book Thinking Fast and Slow. Why This Matters In the context of explanation, Systems 1 and 2 have real power because they show that explanations can fail for two very different reasons.
Further, thinking doesn’t happen in a pipeline, but in a progression. Nevertheless, there is compelling evidence that dual process theory captures important patterns in how we think.
